History:
• Chief complaint: Sensation of chest “tightness” for ~3 hours today.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild shortness of breath (worse on stairs, none at rest), wheeze, non-productive cough. No frank chest pain, no sputum, no hemoptysis, no fever reported.  
• Recent history: Viral “cold” one week ago (sore throat, runny nose, now improving); cough has persisted.  
• Triggers/alleviating factors: Exertion (stairs) increases SOB; has not used usual inhalers for the past week because they ran out.  
• Previous similar episodes: Severe asthma exacerbation at age 16–17 requiring intubation and several-day hospital stay; no recent hospitalizations.  
• Patient goal: Ensure current episode is managed and avoid another severe exacerbation.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma (childhood-onset).  
• Allergic rhinitis/hay fever; dust allergy.  
• Childhood eczema; remote milk-protein allergy.  
• No known drug allergies.  
• Family history: Father—asthma; Mother—eczema.  
• Medications (all currently out of supply):  
  – Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler, dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  – Beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler, dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Surgical/Hospitalizations: Intubation for asthma exacerbation age ~16–17.  
• Social history: University student; smoking/alcohol status not recorded.

Physical Examination:
(Tele-consultation; no in-person exam)  
• Appearance: Conversing in full sentences; not short of breath at rest.  
• Respiratory: Reports wheeze and chest tightness; no objective auscultation performed.  
• Cardiovascular, HEENT, Abdomen, Extremities, Skin, Neuro: Not recorded.  
• Vitals: Not recorded.

Impression:
Acute asthma exacerbation precipitated by recent viral URI and lapse in controller therapy.  
Alternative considerations (consistent with transcript):  
1. Post-viral reactive airways/acute bronchitis – less likely; wheeze better explained by asthma.  
2. Community-acquired pneumonia – unlikely without fever, sputum, or pleuritic pain.

Management Plan:
• Prescriptions sent electronically:  
  – Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler (SABA).  
  – Beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler (ICS).  
  – Spacer device with usage instructions.  
• Oral steroids: 5-day course (two tablets each morning; exact drug and dose not documented). Counselled on possible side-effects (mood change, hyperglycaemia, rash, nausea, headache).  
• Inhaler regimen once recovered: Beclomethasone daily; Salbutamol PRN.  
• Red-flag advice: If Salbutamol needed more frequently than every 3 hours, or any worsening SOB at rest, chest pain, light-headedness—seek urgent medical attention/ER assessment.  
• Work/school: Advised rest and self-certified sick leave up to 7 days if needed.  
• Follow-up: Recommended to contact GP/clinic if no improvement after steroid course or sooner if deterioration.

Patient Summary:
26-year-old man with known asthma ran out of both reliever and controller inhalers one week ago; after a recent URI he developed 3-hour episode of chest tightness, wheeze, and exertional SOB—consistent with an acute asthma flare. Provided rescue/controller inhalers, spacer, and short steroid taper; instructed on red-flag symptoms and follow-up.

Key Takeaways:
• Start oral steroid course immediately; take two tablets each morning for 5 days.  
• Resume daily Beclomethasone and use Salbutamol as needed—seek care if Salbutamol needed more often than every 3 hours.  
• Use spacer with each inhaler puff to improve medication delivery.

Next Steps:
• Obtain medications within the next hour and begin therapy today.  
• Monitor symptoms; arrange GP review or repeat tele-consultation if not improving in 3–5 days.  
• Consider peak-flow meter for home monitoring at follow-up.
